source: TMUA 2023 · Paper 2 · Question 16 · Official worked answer
label: TMUA 2023 · Paper 2 · Question 16
knowledgePattern: Propagate divisibility through an additive recurrence and disprove stronger gcd claims
solution:
Write a=7r,b=7s, with r,s coprime positive integers. Since each new term is the sum of two multiples of 7, it remains a multiple of 7; the recurrence can be continued with this property at every step. I is true.

II is false. Take a=14,b=7, whose HCF is 7. The initial term a is not a factor of b. But the terms begin 14,7,21,28, and the fourth term 28 is a multiple of a, with index greater than 1.

III is false. Take a=21,b=7, again with HCF 7. The terms begin 21,7,28,35,63, and the HCF of a=21 and the fifth term 63 is 21, not 7.

I only: answer B.

hints.title: Track the shared divisor
hints.body: Write the initial values as 7 times integers and see what the recurrence does to a common factor.
hints.recap: A recurrence invariant is a property preserved by every update once it holds initially.
hints.pitfall: A shared factor does not mean it is the greatest common factor of every later pair.
hints.pause: Check which divisibility statement follows at every step.

recall.reminder: A recurrence invariant is a property preserved by every update once it holds initially.

hints.title: Test the stronger claims
hints.body: Generate a few terms symbolically in terms of a,b. Then choose small allowed starting pairs to test the assertions about particular indices.
hints.recap: One counterexample satisfying every premise refutes a universal statement.
hints.pitfall: Keep the initial HCF exactly 7, not merely a multiple of 7.
hints.pause: Check the premise of each implication and the HCF condition for every trial.

recall.reminder: One counterexample satisfying every premise refutes a universal statement.
